utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for the Defence. General Krstic is not here as far as I can see. Mr. Petrusic, can you tell us about the reasons for his absence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. On Friday I notified you of the possibility of General Krstic undergoing a medical examination which was supposed to take place last week but was cancelled. So General Krstic is having his medical checkup today, and that is mainly the reason of his absence from the trial, from the hearing today. He has given a written approval, a written waiver, so that the hearing can continue in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Good morning General Radinovic. I hope that you have managed to have some rest and that you have spent a nice weekend here in The Hague. We're now going to continue with the hearing of your testimony. Mr. Cayley will continue his cross-examination, and let me remind you once again of the necessity to be as brief as possible and as concise as possible in your answers so that we can finish your cross-examination as soon as possible. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, learned counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Cayley: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Now, General, just to refresh your memory as to where we were at the end of last week, we were dealing with the movement of the civilian population from Potocari, and we had discussed at some length the involvement of the Drina Corps Command in that operation, and you've made your comments on those particular facts. Now what I'd like to do is move ahead and discuss another assertion that you make in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Usher, if this could be placed on the ELMO, page 42.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May we have the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, D160 is the General's report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, General, if you wish to reference it, it is also on page 42 in your version, and it is the last sentence on page 42. Now, at the end of paragraph 6.6 you state, and I'll quote, "But here it is important to note and conclude that what happened was not forced movement or deportation, but only the fulfilment of necessary conditions for a movement which that population itself wished." General, do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I am convinced that from the moment of the arrival of the population in Potocari until the beginning of the moving out of the population, there was no coercion whatsoever. The initiative was one of the civilian representatives, and the VRS took it upon itself to organise that moving out of the population on the basis of the attitude and the request made by the representative of the civilian population from Potocari, that is, from Srebrenica. The very process of movement or, rather, the initiative was the one of the civilian representatives of the Muslim population in Srebrenica. It was not the plan of the VRS. And the movement was not a forcible one. On the basis, of course, of the documents that I had access to that was the conclusion that I reached, and I think that I mentioned that fact in the previous sentence. Of course, the fear on the part of the population did play a certain role in this. It's not a new phenomenon. It's actually a rather common phenomenon in every war, including the one that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The population moved from all of the areas that had fallen under the control of the opposing party and Serbs and Croats also moved from such areas. It's a very common phenomenon in any civilian war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, the Judges have heard a number of witnesses who were either Dutch Battalion personnel who were engaged in these events, in the movement of the population, and they've heard from a number of Muslim witnesses, and I'm not going to go through all of those witnesses with you, but one particular witness whose evidence I would like to read you is, in fact, one of the civilian representatives who attended the meeting in Bratunac on the 12th of July of 1995 where General Radinovic and General Krstic were present. She was asked a question by the President in respect of a comment made to her by General Mladic and the question went like this: "Q. Whilst you were at the meeting with General Mladic, at one point he told you that you could choose between surviving and vanishing, and you said that 'vanish' could, in a way, also include the possibility of survival somehow. What I would like to know is whether this possibility of survival was a conclusion of yours or was it General Mladic who had actually said that?" And her answer was: "A. Well, he simply said, 'You can survive or vanish.' My conclusion was that if I leave I would be saved and if I stayed I would die." Now, General, you would agree with me that if an individual is given the impression which they believe that if they stay they are going to be killed and if they leave they will survive, that is not voluntary conduct, is it? That is not an individual exercising their free will to live the enclave, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That statement is completely contrary to the statement which was made by General Mladic in his address to the civilian population in Potocari which was recorded on video footage. He expressly said that they were free to choose whether to leave or to stay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you're not answering the question. Today you're going to be direct, and you're going to be brief, and you're going to answer my questions. We'll get on to General Mladic's statement to the people in Potocari awhile later. What I'm asking you, and you've read evidence from this case, does this woman appear to be voluntarily choosing to leave the enclave? Would you interpret what she said to the President as her making a choice, exercising her own free will to leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: She did have a choice as to whether to stay or to leave. On the basis of all of the documents that I had an opportunity to study, they were given the possibility of choosing whether to stay or to leave. That witness, she probably understood that if she stayed that she would be in some kind of danger. That is how all civilians felt in all of the areas where fighting was going on. That's nothing particularly new. They were all afraid if they should remain under the authority which they did not perceive as theirs. So that is the source of fear and fear is a common consequence of every war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I didn't wish to interrupt my learned colleague Mr. Cayley. However, I should like to ask him when quoting from the transcript to tell us which page he's talking about so that we could follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies, Mr. Visnjic. It was, in fact, page 1135 of the LiveNote transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you mentioned General Mladic giving this television presentation in front of the refugees at Potocari and in essence, as you stated, saying that they could choose to stay or leave. What I would like to address with you is what General Mladic actually thought about the situation and what he was actually stating to other VRS officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 445.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry to interrupt you, but I should like to ask a question of General Radinovic while we're waiting for the document. General, you said that the moving out of the population was a common feature of the war in Bosnia. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That's an understatement, Mr. President. I don't know what would be the equivalent term. A "common feature," a "common phenomenon" is a rather mild word. I just said that it was something very common, that it was a rule in every such situation, in every civil war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. I should like to know whether the displacement was a cause of the war or a consequence of the war, that is to say whether the displacement was an objective of the war or a consequence of the war. What is your opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: My opinion is that it was a consequence of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is your position. Thank you, General Radinovic. Mr. Cayley, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in order to save your voice, I will read this intercept. It is an intercepted communication between General Mladic and an unidentified person dated the 12th of July, and the conversation proceeded as follows: X: Go ahead, General. M: Have these buses and trucks left? X: They have. M: When? X: Ten minutes ago. M: Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to and those who don't want to. X: I understand General. M: Don't issue any statements and don't interrupt them over the radio station. We'll open a corridor towards Kladanj. X: ....... M: Indeed, let it pass there. Take a patrol of ours to wait on the road and remove the mines and obstacles. Leave the territory. X: Yes, General. Now, you would agree with me here, General, that General Mladic is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. expressing the view that everybody has got to leave the enclave, all of the Muslim population, in his own words, "Those who want to and those who don't"; isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: My findings are based not on intercepts but on reliable sources, that is, operational documents which constitute primary sources in my studies, and I am quite certain that they give a relatively reliable picture on the situation on the ground. Second, my testimony and my conclusions are also based on doctrinary principles which are not subject to revision. I am using the information, the knowledge of the military science, and I am using the relevant methodology. Intercepts are unreliable sources in several senses, and I couldn't use them as the basis for my conclusions because we have only the transcript and not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, and I'm -- I can read it out to you if you want, but on page 11 of your report you state that you relied on primary sources, and you included intercepted conversations within that list of primary sources. So in your report you have indicated that you have relied on them, so I will repeat the question to you again. You can deal with the reliability or unreliability of them in the re-examination with Mr. Visnjic. I want you to answer this simple question: If, if General Mladic said this statement recorded in this intercept, does it not indicate that he was giving no choice to the population, to the Muslim population of Srebrenica? He was basically stating everybody has got to go, wasn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: You have Mladic's statements which are completely contrary to this. I don't know which source you wish to consider as primary or not. You have Mladic's statement which was given publicly before the cameras, in front of his officers and in front of everybody who were present there, giving freedom of choice to the population there; that is, that they were not forced to leave, that those who wanted to stay would be guaranteed safety, as was the case with the Serbian population. And then on the other hand you have a source which you consider to be reliable. I happen not to consider them reliable. I did take them into account. I studied them, those intercepts, but I never referred to them because I do not consider them to be reliable, and I think I have enough reasons to doubt their reliability when it comes to reaching conclusions. So you have two kinds of evidence: You have Mladic who is addressing the population, telling them that they are free to stay and that they would not be harmed; and on the other hand, you have this piece of paper which you have just shown me on the basis of which one could perhaps conclude that Mladic wanted them to leave. My conclusions are not based on intercepts but on documents whose reliability can be ascertained. I did not reach my conclusions on the basis of this. I made my findings on the basis of Mladic's address to the local population, and from that address I was not able to conclude that he wanted to force the population to leave Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on page 11 of your report, and you don't need to make reference to it, you state, "This expert testimony was written using numerous primary and secondary sources." You then give an entire list of all the primary sources, and in the primary sources are listed "intercepted conversations." General, is it your normal practice when you are putting together any kind of report that you quote a primary source for your report which you believe to be completely unreliable? Is that your normal practice as an academic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, as any serious expert, I am duty-bound to inform the user of my report the types of sources that I was using. Intercepts are by all means primary sources, but only those intercepts that can be authenticated and identified. I am sure that you studied my report most seriously, but you can see that in my report I did not rely on any of the intercepts. And I have studied all of the intercepts that had been made available to the Defence, but I did not rely on them because I do not deem them to be reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your report speaks for itself, General. If we can move on, please, to Prosecutor's Exhibit 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Will you just excuse me? General Radinovic, as a historic witness, you, do you think that the public statements are a reliable source in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, Your Honour, that not all public statements can be considered as 100 per cent reliable. Of course, one has to bear in mind a certain kind of public image, but I divide them in two groups. In one group I can place the statements which are publicly addressed and which -- whose authenticity can be ascertained and those statements whose authenticity cannot be verified, and I will always rely myself on the first group of the documents. And I understand what it was that you meant in your question. I understand all of the limitations of such statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is the statement that you referred to in your evidence in-chief, and it is the statement that was signed by Major Franken, Mr. Mandzic from the Muslim community, and Miroslav Deronjic who, as you already stated, was appointed by Mr. Karadzic to the civilian commissioner in Srebrenica. Now, I wish to address some of the paragraphs with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if it could be placed on the ELMO. If you could please move it up a little, Mr. Usher. Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you will see in the version you have, and this is about halfway down the page, "At the end of the negotiations between the two sides the following was agreed: that our civilian population could stay in the enclave or move out, depending on the wish of each individual." Now, General, Major Franken, a signatory to this document has given evidence before the Judges about the meaning of that particular phrase and this is what he states, and he refers to the public statement made by General Mladic about giving the population a free choice, and this is what he says: "I understand that General Mladic made that statement, but hardly any realistic statement because the fate of those who wanted to stay, even if they could, was, let's say, uncertain, and in the end there was not a choice. Mladic ordered the population to go to Kladanj, period." Now, General, you would agree with me that a signatory to this document, a man who is actually present during these events, would better know than you whether or not the population was actually given a choice as to whether they could stay or leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As an honourable professional who signed this record and allowed that in the first paragraph, "We find this position that our civilian population could stay in the enclave or move out depending on the wish of each individual," how can that be explained then? How could the Major, as an honourable officer with ethics, sign a document while thinking what he's stated, as you quoted him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me tell you why, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That speaks of something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me tell you immediately why, and we'll come back to my question on that. The reason, General, why he signed this statement, and he gave evidence to this Court to that effect, is that the lives of 59 individuals depended on him signing this statement. That is the evidence that he gave to this Court. It was intimated to him by the Bosnian Serb authorities that if he did not sign this document those people's lives would be at risk. Wounded Muslims in a hospital in Bratunac. Now I'll ask you again, General. You would agree with me that Major Franken would have a better idea than you as to whether or not the population was actually given a choice as to whether or not to leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: In answer to that question of yours, sir, the best answer is what the Major has signed. He signed a statement claiming that the Muslim population had the choice of staying in Srebrenica or moving out. I cannot answer your question on the basis of anything other than the document I have here in front of me which you have given me as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider Major Franken's evidence to this Court when you came to your opinion about this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I studied all the testimony, everything that the Defence had at its disposal. I cannot, of course, remember each and every detail. I would have to refresh my memory and look through the statement. But of course I do remember the testimony you are referring to. The testimony of all professional officers who were in Srebrenica make me very angry as a soldier, as a professional. I cannot understand that they could have done one thing and stated another. They should have behaved with far greater responsibility, in a far more professional manner, with greater determination, with greater courage, of course with risks because the military profession is a high-risk profession, and it was particularly risky in Srebrenica in a civil war. And this was a risk that they should have taken upon themselves, and they should have signed only what they were quite confident of rather than signing documents that allegedly they were coerced into doing. And I cannot believe that that was the case, because this document is here with us until time immemorial. It is a historical document. It is a document I have to trust. I do take note also of the testimony given by the Major, but for me this is more important, more reliable document than what he said later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, excuse me for interrupting you. You remember seeing pictures of General Mladic distributing sweets to the children in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know why he did that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I personally think that General Mladic, like any other human being, has emotions and that the situation in which the population found itself as a result of combat operations was such that this had to move him as it would any person, and, personally, I think that he did this exclusively out of emotional reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we have many witnesses who have told us that these sweets were later taken away. For a moment while the cameras were on these sweets were distributed. When the cameras were removed these sweets were taken away again. Do you have anything to make regarding the authenticity of these pictures for history, the camera pictures or the other pictures that the camera did not record from the standpoint of authenticity for history?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I really cannot absolutely imagine that General Mladic could distribute sweets while on camera and then to take them away again. This is simply something that I cannot accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have already said you're an expert witness, a military witness. It is similar to this situation. You have a document and you have a testimony. You have a document, a TV picture, and testimony. You say, "The document, for me, is the truth. I don't want to know about the testimony." In relation to the question I have put to you, you're telling us, "No. I don't believe that General Mladic could have taken away the sweets afterwards." Why? Because you have a picture? No. We too have testimony about that. So this is a question of authenticity. From your standpoint, which is the real source of history? For you the picture is what counts, the document, whereas testimony is not worth anything. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. No. I did not mean the testimony is not worth anything. But comparing the probative value, for me as a person making conclusions -- I am not talking as a jurist, of course. If I have to make conclusions as to what happened over there, then for me there is no doubt that a certain individual did give candy to a certain population, as this was recorded by camera. So this is a document that cannot be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the question is "Why?" What was the objective of that? What was the aim? Why did General Mladic say, "You can stay or leave. It's up to you to choose"? Also, what was the objective he had in mind distributing the sweets and then taking them away again? When one is interpreting a source such as a document, one needs to interpret it in terms of the objective behind that document. So in your analysis, did you try to find the objective, to answer the question "Why?"

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I was going to say that to Your Honour but was interrupted. There is no doubt that General Mladic did distribute sweets before the cameras. Perhaps I would equally value testimony if General Mladic was to collect the sweets. But if some irresponsible individual did it, then that kind of behaviour cannot be attributed to General Mladic. If this were to be done to General Mladic, then perhaps one could ask what the intention was when he gave those sweets. But if somebody else did that, then it is not General Mladic's intention that is in question but the intention of the person who did it. So I think that General Mladic had no other objective but to distribute those sweets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have just one question. In your conclusion that this movement of the civilian population was a voluntary one, do you include the men in that? In other words, the women and children, as you know - I think there is no dispute - were put on buses and moved on toward Kladanj. The men were not, at least the men who were in the normal ages, not elderly, were not allowed on the buses and they were taken off. We won't talk about what happened to them, but they were taken off to one side and something happened to them. But is it your position that they had a choice? They could have stayed in Srebrenica? I mean the testimony is uniform, uniform, that they are taken off and something was done to them in -- both in Potocari and later on. But would you say that regardless of how you view the women and children who got on the bus and went on to Kladanj, would you say those young men had a choice?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, Prosecutor's Exhibit 47. Put yourself for one moment in the position of Major Franken. It's the 17th of July. The entire civilian population, 30.000 people, are, to the best of his knowledge, safely out of the enclave. Fifty-nine wounded Muslim men remain in the hospital. The Bosnian Serb army is in control. He is informed their welfare depends on your signature on this document. To save those people, you have to sign this document. What would a military officer of honour and integrity have done in that situation? Would he have refused to sign and put those people at risk?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It's a dilemma. I was not in that dilemma at the time, so I don't know what my decision would have been. The question has been put out of context. One could answer that question only if one found one's self in that situation. I'm a person who would -- I'm not saying that is the pattern of behaviour that others would have to follow, including the Major. I'm a person who would not sell his honour and integrity for anything in the world, even his own life or the life of his own family. I would not sign anything dishonourable. There is no force in the world that could make me sign something that I consider dishonourable. To sign that something was done properly, knowing that it was not done properly, for me that is something terrible. It is a moral fall. I would not permit myself to make it. There is no fear in the world that would make me sign something like that. Maybe that would be irrational, unreasonable. I grant you that the Major may have out of fear done so, but I would not have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General, you wouldn't consider signing it under the circumstances, and at the first opportunity denounce it as being under great pressure? Wouldn't you consider that as an attitude, as a honest approach to reconcile saving lives and being honest? Just for the sake of your statement.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have done many things prior to this to avoid getting into this situation. I would have been in control of the whole process with much greater responsibility and with much greater risk than they were ready to expose themselves to. I know that this activity of escorting this process of displacement and adjusting it to the rules that could have been implemented at the time, I know that that was very difficult and highly risky, but that was the primordial role that they had, that it was their duty, and that is what they should have done; and then it would have been known immediately if there were irregularities, and there were apparently, then it would have been known there and then had these gentlemen carried out their duty. And there is no other way I can react to this act of theirs. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me just read another portion from the statement. It's on the ELMO. "It was arranged that the evacuation would be carried out by the army and police of Republika Srpska, and that UNPROFOR would supervise and provide an escort for the evacuation." Let's examine for a moment, General, what actually happened on the ground, and let me read you first of all the testimony of Witness G who was a Dutch soldier tasked with escorting the convoys, and he was asked a question by my learned friend Mr. Harmon. "Witness G, did it appear to you that the theft of your vehicles, your two vehicles, and the theft of the other escort vehicles was organised?" The witness here is discussing how when he went to escort a convoy, vehicles were stolen. The vehicles were stolen from the escort at gunpoint. He goes on to say: "Yes, it seemed to me that that was the case."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give the Judges your opinion as to why you think the escort vehicles were being taken?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Those escort vehicles were used by us to follow the buses, to escort the buses, and it seemed to me that the Bosnian Serbs just didn't want to see, didn't want to see what happened to the buses and the content of the buses. That is why, usually with violence, they took away our vehicles. Now, General, it's a fact, isn't it, that the Dutch couldn't escort the refugees because they were prevented from doing so at gunpoint by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. No, that is not correct. That is not true. That is not how a convoy is escorted. That is not how that job is organised. A person -- the person, who wanted to provide effective escort and to control the whole process effectively, and that was the obligation of the Dutch Battalion, that person should have made sure that in every vehicle there should have been a Dutch soldier, rather than one vehicle in the whole column. And then, because of poor communications, the convoy's drawn out, a vehicle breaks down or intentionally something happens --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: -- situations which can be foreseen in similar circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not answering the question. Were you aware, were you aware, General, from reading the evidence in this case, that Dutch soldiers, travelling in pairs, armed, in an escort vehicle, were prevented from carrying out their duty by the VRS at gunpoint? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I read the testimony to that effect, and if that really happened in the way they testified, of course I do not accept such behaviour, but I'm saying that there was a way to prevent that if the Dutch Battalion had carried out the operation as it should have been done. Therefore, they, too, contributed to the irregularity of the whole process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read to you, General, Major Franken, his evidence, the Deputy Commander of the Dutch Battalion, what he said about the escorts. When he's referring to "activity" in his evidence, he's referring to the escort duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many vehicles did you lose to this activity that you recall?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: In total, we lost about 33 vehicles, but I think concerning the convoys it would be about 15 or 16 jeeps. But the figures are somewhere in the documents, the exact figures, but that's what I recall now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think that they were taking the jeeps? Why were they stopping the Dutch escorts from accompanying the buses?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Because they didn't want anybody to be around; that's obvious. Otherwise, they can't think of any reason to stop them because we were not a threat. We were not a military potential. One jeep with two guys in it is nonsense, and so obviously they didn't want us to witness whatever would happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you'd lost 16 jeeps, did you think that there was any kind of significance or planning that somebody had actually decided that this was to happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It was obvious that the word was out to frustrate the convoy escort and the regular forces as far as we could judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that's on page 2031.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, it's a fact that the Bosnian Serb army had already decided to frustrate the Dutch escorts as soon as the convoys moved out, hadn't it? That was part of the plan.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, it was not part of the plan. Those are incidents, and those to blame for the incidents are both the command of the Dutch Battalion that did not plan the whole operational activity as it did. They have enormous responsibility. I am not justifying any single incident or any single crime committed along the route, but among other things, it was due to the improper implementation of that activity. The Dutch Battalion should have planned the escort in the proper way, which means in every vehicle there should be a soldier at the head of the column vehicle, and a vehicle at the tail-end of the column, and then this would not have happened. So the incidents and individual criminal behaviour by members of the army and the police of Republika Srpska along the route of the column which occurred as testified by the member of the Dutch Battalion would not have happened if the whole activity had been carried out properly. Of course, this does not relieve of responsibility the perpetrators, but I am claiming that it was not the plan of the army of Republika Srpska. Nor do I accept that part of the plan was to frustrate the escort, but because that escort was not planned and implemented as it should have been, then various irregularities occurred which enabled various criminal acts which I am opposed to with my whole being, which I condemn even more fiercely than you because I as a member of that nation carry part of the stigma, and every honourable Serb carries a part of that stain, that stigma, and it will take a long time to rid ourselves of that. I do not justify it; I am just explaining how it came to pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General, just to cut a long story short, I'm not speaking of sense of duty or even being a hero, but could these DutchBat soldiers, being a small minority, if they insisted on fulfilling their duty, which you highly recommended, could they have practically succeeded? Could two soldiers come into a bus while the Bosnian Serb army is preventing them? Is it a practical possibility even if they were, as you said, they had to fulfil their duty? On a strictly practical level was it possible facing an army?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that activity of escort is an activity that is studied in military schools. And if it is not studied, it is part of common sense. It is the obligation of the escort to escort the column out in the most effective way, and one of those ways is by an escort being in the vehicle to check who is getting in and coming out. And even if he was not in a position to prevent, he at least could have seen who did it. I am quite certain that if that activity had been done in the way I'm saying is it should have been done, then there would certainly have been at least fewer such crimes. I can't say that there wouldn't have been any. And as an individual, I am very sorry that it was not done, but I'm not giving an excuse to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Judge Riad and Your Honours, there is actually-- we won't go into it now. There is actually evidence to that effect, that there was insufficient personnel, but I think we can probably deal with that in closing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in your report - and I won't refer to it because time is marching on - you essentially state that the UN was a party to this movement of the population and that they also, in a sense, are partly to blame for what happened in Srebrenica. What I want to ask you is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if Prosecutor's Exhibit 113/3 could be placed on the ELMO, please. If you could move it up, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a press release by the Security Council of the United Nations on the 14th of July of 1995. I won't read all of it, but what I will read, the fourth paragraph down. "'The Council is deeply concerned about ongoing forced relocation of tens of thousands of civilians from the Srebrenica safe areas to the Tuzla region by the Bosnian Serb party,' said a presidential statement of the Security Council. "'Such a forced relocation is a clear violation of the human rights of the civilian population,' the statement added. "The Council reaffirmed that those who had committed or had ordered the commission of `ethnic cleansing' would be held individually responsible." General, are you aware that Security Council of the United Nations, the day after the deportation was complete, issued a public statement to the world criminalising that conduct? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I cannot remember at this point, but I'm sure I follow that and I know that such statements were made. However, I can tell you now that the movement of the population from Srebrenica was not -- it did not constitute ethnic cleansing or plan. It was a consequence of war activities which in turn is a consequence of a fear of having to remain under the control of an authority they do not identify as theirs. It's a common phenomenon. It's a rule. Serbs moved out from the territories under Muslim and Croat controls, and Croats moved out from the territory under Muslim control, under Serb control, and the other way around. So all three sides left certain areas. That can apply to all three warring factions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me read for you Prosecutor's Exhibit 113/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If that could be placed on the ELMO, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm only going to read the fourth paragraph of this. This is a statement made on the day that the movement of the population was complete, and it's a statement by Sadako Ogata, then the UN High Commissioner for Refugees. "In Geneva, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, called the wholesale removal of Srebrenica residents one of the most blatant examples of ethnically motivated forced displacement we have seen yet in war. 'It is inconceivable to me that the Bosnian Serbs can inflict such hardship on the people of Srebrenica, people who have already endured years of war and suffering,' said Ogata in a statement." General, based on your report in which you say that the UN was a party to this movement of the population, are you stating that the High Commissioner for Refugees and the Security Council were criminalising conduct to which the UN itself was a party?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Is Mr. Akashi considered to be a member of that mechanism? I think so. The mechanism of the United Nations. He was the one who sent a telegram to the Security Council in New York proposing an agreement to be reached with the Serbian side concerning the movement of the population in accordance with their wishes, that is, as it was expressed by the Muslim representatives of the civilians from Srebrenica requested as early as the 9th of July. That cannot be disputed. On the basis of that, one can conclude the mechanism of the United Nations indeed took part in that. Certain members, members of the Dutch Battalion, for example, as UN forces who were deployed in Srebrenica, they were also party to that process. I didn't say that the Security Council participated in it and reached decisions to that effect. I was referring to the representatives of the United Nations who were delegated to act such in the territory of the former Yugoslavia including the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They took part in the process, and they cannot be relieved of a portion of responsibility for everything that occurred as a consequence of that act. If we ignore that aspect of culpability, I'm afraid that we might be faced with similar problems in the future. So one really needs to say clearly who is guilty of what, who is to blame of what. What it seems to me as the most significant point is that one should take into account the fact that it was not a political plan of the VRS to ethnically cleanse Srebrenica because before that, in 1993, 10.000 people moved out from Srebrenica also on the request and nobody considered it to be an incident of ethnic cleansing. All of the Serbian population moved out from the valley of Neretva River. There is not a single Serb living in that area. Likewise, the town of Mostar, there are no Serbs left in that town and nobody's talking about ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry, but we must move on. There were crimes committed against the Serbian people. Nobody denies that. But that is not relevant to these proceedings. Let us move on. Now, General, you stated both in your evidence and in your report that it is a legitimate military operation to check the identities of male Muslims who are passing through the hands of the VRS, and I think you stated in your evidence that the Bratunac Brigade had indeed provided a list of suspected war criminals to the Drina Corps headquarters. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, as Her Honour Judge Wald has already stated, there has been a great deal of evidence in this case that men and boys were separated by the Bosnian army in Potocari and that, it appears, was in the form of an organised military operation. The Prosecutor does not dispute the legitimacy of checking Muslim males for war crimes, but I want to deal with another aspect of this operation. First of all, I want to read to you a description given by Captain van Duijn, then a young platoon commander with the Dutch army who describes the state of the men and boys who had been separated in Potocari, and this is what he said:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the appearance of those men that you saw at the White House?" And the White House is the location where these individuals were separated.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: They were packed together. Because it was very warm, they were sweating. They were very, very, very scared. Some of them were shivering. Some of the men were speaking to themselves but you could easily see that they were very, very scared. This is on page 1768.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: When I came up to the White House, and as you can see in front of the White House there is a large lawn, it was covered totally with personal belongings, with pictures, holiday snaps, as well as passports and other identity papers. The witness then goes on, General, to say that he had a conversation with a VRS officer called Mane about why all of these belongings particularly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: And particularly identification papers had been separated from these individuals and placed in a big pile in front of the White House. And this is the answer that that VRS officer gave about why those individuals, why those Muslims had been separated from their personal belongings and from their identification papers:

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He said, "Well, they don't need the stuff that's there. They don't need it any more." And I asked him how he could explain the fact that if they wanted to know who was a war criminal and who was not they could do that without identity papers, because if they would give a false name, it wouldn't be on the list of war criminals and the person would go free and join the rest of the convoy to Tuzla. And he more or less laughed at me and said, "Well, don't make such a fuss out of it. They just don't need their passports any more."

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Prosecutor's Exhibit 62 could be made ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can you explain to the Judges why, if it was a requirement of the Security and Intelligence Service to identify these people for the purposes of alleged war crimes, that the Bosnian Serb army was systematically removing all forms of identification from these Muslim men and boys?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: In my report, I stated that the identity checkups of males was a legitimate activity. There were lists of war crimes suspects in Srebrenica. That list was there. Of course one still has to find out whether it was only a suspicion or whether those people were really war criminals. However, one can justify the procedure of checking up the identity of males who had arrived in Potocari, namely, whether their names can be found on the list of suspects of war crimes against the Serbian population. Moreover, whether any of them was a member of the 28th Division, that is, whether they had been engaged in fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the Prosecutor doesn't dispute anything of what you've just said, as I informed you just a moment ago. The question I have for you: Why was the Bosnian Serb army removing forms of identification from these Muslim men and boys who had been separated in Potocari? Why, if they needed to identify these people they were removing their passports and their identification cards from them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Of course, before I can answer your question, one has to see who it was who did it, whether it was done by the members of the army or someone else. I didn't -- I wasn't able to reach a full answer to that question, whether it was done by members of the army or members of the police. For me as a military expert, that is not the same. Second, as regards the question whether individuals were engaged in such conduct without any authorisation or whether it was based on a preconceived plan, I do not have any information. I do not have any evidence to that effect. You say members of the VRS. If indeed we are talking about the members of the VRS, we are talking about individuals, and individual members of the overall system of the VRS. We do not -- I do not have a single piece of evidence which would enable me to conclude that it was done on the basis of a preconceived plan issued by the command system, that is, that the Muslim population should be destroyed in that way. I cannot confirm your allegation that it was done in a systematic way by the army. If that indeed was done, it was done by individuals. And of course, I do not consider it to be legitimate. I consider it to be a crime, and I, of course, cannot justify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I according to your assessment, was the situation under control, or was everything running wild and everything was doing what -- everybody could do anything. If there was a control, then there would be discipline and, as you say, a systematic attitude; or was it anarchy, according to your assessment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, I must say, Your Honour, that there are enough elements to consider that system not to be adequate and proper at that time. It was rather chaotic. First of all, a very large group of Muslim population suddenly appeared in and around Potocari, which was rather unexpected in terms of the restricted character of the Srebrenica operation. And the Drina Corps Command was faced with that situation without being adequately prepared. They couldn't promptly deal with it. At the same time in the night between the 11th and the 12th, and on the 12th of July certainly, certain elements which did not belong to the Drina Corps appeared in the area, namely, the special brigade of the MUP and certain forces of the Main Staff of the VRS, each acting within their own competencies and without a very strict system of subordination. That is, all of a sudden, we have several lines of command in a very restricted area. So that certainly affected the effectiveness of the whole operation, and it is very difficult to lay the blame either on the army or the police. Judging by all this, the situation must have been very chaotic in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Whenever there is army and the police, don't they have the same command? Would it be to the most senior officer or command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That principle is in force only in the areas where combat operations are taking place. Since the operation for Srebrenica had come to an end, that system was no longer in force strictly speaking. Police forces of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska were not under the control of the Drina Corps Command, and there wasn't a single document on the basis of which the Drina Corps would have -- the Drina Corps Command would have authority to control the conduct of the members of the special brigade of the MUP which appeared in the area as early as on the 12th of July. And practically speaking, they were controlling the area around Potocari and establishing control also on the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje. And the VRS, that is, the Drina Corps, its units did not function -- did not control that particular portion of the territory. And in view of that, it is very difficult to state firmly who it was who engaged in this unauthorised activity of separating men from women and children, and the whole illegal procedure that followed from then on. So I do not have any basis to claim with certainty as to who it was who engaged in that activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if you could look at the photograph that you can see on the screen in front of you, and this is a photograph that was taken by a DutchBat member sometime after the 13th of July. And these are all of the belongings of the Muslim men and boys who had been separated, their belongings, their identification cards; and as you can see, there is a fire. It's being burnt. He gave evidence that it was burned by the Bosnian Serbs. Now, General, you would agree with me that if you wanted to leave no trace of somebody's existence, a very effective way of doing that is to remove all forms of identification that that person had ever possessed.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but Bosnian Serbs include civilians, policemen, and soldiers. The issue is, who it was who done it. I'm not trying to justify --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, answer the question. Do you or do you not agree with me that if you wanted to leave no trace of somebody's existence, a very effective way of doing that would be to remove their identification and then destroy it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: On this photograph, I can only see that the area is on fire, but I don't know who did it, why they did it, when they did it. I cannot answer your question on the basis of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you've considered all of the evidence in this case. You're the expert. The Judges have heard evidence that these men and boys' identification papers were systematically removed and destroyed. That evidence has been heard in this courtroom. Do you or do you not agree with me that the reason why that was done was to leave no trace of these people's existence; that is the reason why these identity cards were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The very fact of seizing such documents cannot in itself constitute a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not the question, General. That is not the question. And I'm going to insist on an answer. You can decline to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, you can try perhaps once again, and we will see what the General's answer will be. General, I think that you fully understand the question. We will give you one more opportunity to answer it. Mr. Cayley, just once more, last time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people's passports and identification papers were destroyed as a step in essentially leaving no trace of their life or existence; isn't that right, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Those who did it committed a criminal act; however, the whole process is not only that. The seizure of documents does not necessarily constitute a prohibited act. Those who did it, those who burned it, must be held responsible; and the issue is to know the identity of that person and the reasons for that. There are several aspects to this problem which can be mutually exclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, would this be a convenient time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I want to leave deportation fairly swiftly or, as in your words, the movement of the population, but first of all and finally on this area, I would like to read to you what General Krstic told us in a police interview with the Office of the Prosecutor regarding the movement of the population. General, prior to your evidence did you speak with General Krstic at all in respect of your expert report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Krstic provided with a copy of your report, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know. I gave a copy to the Defence. I don't know whether they gave it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the General could be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 399/B bis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is, in fact, on page 19, General, of the B/C/S, of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it is page 32, Mr. Usher of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For you, General, it's page 19, so you can follow, but I will read portions of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: This, Mr. President, is the public transcript of General Krstic's interview with Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read out to you, General, what General Krstic stated about the movement of the population. "Now, what is their guilt and their responsibility? General Mladic was in charge of all activity. His guilt also consists of his orders that he gave to the units of the Drina Corps to continue the attack towards Srebrenica, which caused the civilians to flee the town and the villages --"

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you give it to me I can find the relevant page. The B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see where I've placed a blue mark, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Now, what is their guilt and their responsibility?" This is General Krstic speaking. "General Mladic was in charge of all activity. His guilt also consists of his orders that he gave to the units of the Drina Corps to continue the attack towards Srebrenica, which caused the civilians to flee the town and the villages south and west of Srebrenica. When the Drina Corps units entered Srebrenica, there was nobody, it was completely empty. There were no civilians; there were no soldiers. This also can be seen from a videotape, from a film that has been shown on Dutch TV and English and American TV and so on. As I said before, it was General Mladic who ordered the units of Drina Corps to continue the attack towards Bratunac through Potocari. Fortunately, as I explained before, after a lot of arguing we managed to prevent the carrying out of this order so that it would not happen. "As far as the deportation is concerned, since that is the first activity on the list, and this is what I have information on, this is what happened. The deportation took place on the 12th and 13th of July. This was organised, led, and managed by the Commander of the Main Staff, through the senior officers that I have listed. General Mladic was the one who was literally there, commanding the loading of people onto buses. His officers and soldiers from his security unit and a battalion of military police of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, they were the ones who were pulling the men off the buses, after which a security check of these people was carried out by the chief of security administration and security officers who were deployed in this area. I do declare that not a single soldier of the Drina Corps came to the area of Potocari, nor would General Mladic have allowed that, except for those people of his." Now, General, you would agree with me that General Krstic has characterised the movement of the population as deportation and has laid the blame at the door of General Mladic, hasn't he, from this interview?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, that follows from this interview. This is the view of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before you gave your evidence, had you read this interview?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I read the interview, but only after I had written my report. I mean, I didn't know about the existence of this interview for quite some time. And when I completed my report, I had the opportunity of reading the interview, so I know what it contains and I know about this position that he took in respect of that. But again, it's General Krstic's view. He's entitled to have a view of his own. I consider it from a certain distance, but it is very difficult to have a distance in respect of that because we are talking about the events which are very hard, and even for me who tried to analyse the situation objectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, General, your position is such that whereas the accused himself acknowledges the criminality of this conduct, albeit excluding himself from responsibility, you maintain the position as an expert on his behalf that the movement of the population was an entirely voluntary one, that the population decided to move itself?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I'm not Krstic's expert witness; I'm the Court's expert witness, and in view of my knowledge and expertise, I'm trying to understand what happened. And on the basis of that, I compiled my report, and it is on the basis of that that I'm giving my testimony here before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that since Mr. Krstic is the one actually accused of this crime, and since he was actually there at the time, he would know better than you the nature of the movement of the population in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as an objective assessment of the situation is concerned, I don't see any reason why General Krstic should be any more objective than myself. He may have more personal knowledge; however, the analysis of the documents and the overall situation and events does not necessarily constitute an advantage for him. It can also operate to his disadvantage because he's the one who is accused of it. So in view of that, it can operate as some kind of limitation as far as his understanding of the situation is concerned. I don't have a problem of that kind. I am not restricted in my views in my way, and I think that I'm competent enough to have reached the conclusion that I stated in my report and that I'm stating here again before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you thus suggesting to the Court that when General Krstic told the Office of the Prosecutor that this activity was deportation, that he was either incorrect or was lying to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It is, of course, your right to put to me anything you want, but I kindly ask you not to do that. I'm not saying that he lied. I'm just saying that he maybe doesn't fully understand the meaning of the word "deportation." I'm not a jurist either, so I may have problems understanding it as well. The way I interpreted the movement of the population from Srebrenica was that it was a consequence of war activities, the war being a civil one in nature. Second, I also interpret it as their wish to move out, out of fear of consequences that might ensue. Nobody wants to leave their home unless they are frightened of staying. I didn't claim that it was an expression of the free will on the part of that population because the life would be better for them in Tuzla, but because they were fearful of the consequences of the war, they expressed their wish to leave Srebrenica. There is not a single trace of justification in my testimony. I'm just trying to understand the consequences and the causes in an objective way. Whether we should call it a deportation or a movement of the population, I don't know. I'm not an expert to reach such conclusions. All I'm trying to explain here is how such things arrive in any war, and indeed, many such phenomenon took place throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, and many Serbs left many parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you've made the point about the Serbs. It's accepted that the Serbs were also victims in this war, but let's move on. Now, General, I stated to you from the interview of General Krstic that he holds General Mladic responsible for what happened, General Mladic and his officers. You yourself in your report state that the Drina Corps Command was relieved of all responsibility in this operation. Do you agree with General Krstic that General Mladic was responsible for the movement of the population from Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. Not that it was General Mladic but that that part of the activity was not under the control of the Drina Corps, that it was within the competence of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, that's not the question I asked you. I asked you whether or not General Mladic was responsible for the movement of the civilian population from Srebrenica to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: In my report, I didn't discuss the responsibility, the culpability of General Mladic but the responsibility of General Krstic, and I was explicit enough in my report when I stated that General Krstic was not responsible for the operation nor did he conduct it in any way. I did not examine the responsibility of General Mladic or his subordinate officers. I discussed the responsibility of General Krstic, and I discussed it in view of his responsibilities and competencies, the competencies of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you're the military expert. Consider it now. Consider whether General Mladic was responsible now. Do you or do you not agree with General Krstic that it was General Mladic who was responsible for the movement of the population from Srebrenica to Tuzla? Is General Mladic to blame for this activity?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to repeat what I said. In order to fulfil the task that was given to me by this institution, I dealt with the responsibility of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I think you should move on to your next question. You have heard the answer of the witness. The witness is probably going to repeat once again what he has already stated. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General Krstic, in his interview, in essence said that there were a group of officers around General Mladic who had an equal level of responsibility for what happened. He named General Tolimir from the Main Staff as also being responsible for what happened in Srebrenica. Do you agree with General Krstic that General Tolimir was also responsible for the movement of the population from Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Sir, my answer in response to your question is identical to the previous one. I did not deal with the responsibility of anyone else but General Krstic, that is the command system of the Drina Corps, to the extent that General Krstic, in the period between the 11th and the 13th -- 12th and the 13th of July belonged to the chain of command of the Drina Corps and in view of the role he played within that chain of command. In order for me to answer your question, I should study the documents once again in order to provide you with the answer as to the responsibility of other officers for the operation in question. I cannot answer your question. I can just speak about the responsibility of General Krstic because that was the subject matter of my analysis and my findings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, General, your report essentially concentrates only on who was not responsible not who was responsible.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. My report concentrates on an analysis of the activity, and it is focused on the role and responsibility of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, in acknowledging that my statement is incorrect, that in fact it's wrong to say that you didn't concentrate on who was responsible, I'll ask you another question based on the same interview that General Krstic gave and that is this: General Krstic also named Colonel Ljubo Beara from the Main Staff, from the Security Administration of the Main Staff, that he was another officer who was responsible for everything that happened after the 11th of July, 1995, in Srebrenica. Do you agree with General Krstic's statement about Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must object. This has been the third time that my learned colleague is asking his question to General Radinovic. I believe that the subject of this cross-examination is not a further investigation of the subject. I think that General Radinovic has given us enough explanation as to the framework of his analysis in respect of this case. I think that what Mr. Cayley wants him to answer falls outside that framework, and I think it is the subject of an investigation or certain other activities which do not have much to do with the expertise and the testimony of General Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, how do you respond to that objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, ultimately in any criminal case the individual or individuals who are responsible for the crimes alleged is absolutely fundamental. Now, the witness had stated that he has reviewed all of the material that is available in this case. General Krstic makes assertions about individuals on the Main Staff of the VRS who are responsible for what happened. It's absurd to infer to the Court that he has only considered those persons who are not responsible and not the persons who are actually responsible. I'm simply going through the list of individuals who General Krstic states were responsible. I'm asking the witness whether he agrees or disagrees. If he doesn't wish to make a comment, then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there anything you wish to add, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that the issue of who is responsible is a very important one which permeates the whole case, but, Mr. Cayley, I think you're running a risk of receiving one and the same answer to all of your questions. You may now continue, but somehow I suspect that General Radinovic is going to provide you with the same answers. Please continue. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that I know, but at least it will be on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Mr. President, I should like to state the following: I am not avoiding the answer to any of the questions that have been put to me. However, I think I would be acting irresponsibly if I should attempt to state who is responsible since I didn't study, analyse exactly who did what and where General Mladic and other officers were at a certain point in time, what were their messages or their communication. I really do not feel able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Radinovic, we understand your position, but if that is the case, please give us a clear answer. Just tell us that you cannot answer the question, because you're wasting too much time in explaining your inability to answer the question. So you can simply state "Yes or no, I agree or I do not agree" with the statement made by the Prosecutor. If you wish to add a comment, you are free to do so, but first of all give us a clear and direct answer to the question. Answer the question in accordance with your knowledge. If you do not know it, just tell us so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. President, the question that is put to me is a leading one, and it requires a yes or no answer, and I'm not able to give a yes or no answer so I have to explain why. I'm not trying to avoid answering the question. I should like the Prosecutor not to ask such questions of me, but to concentrate on the issue of General Krstic's responsibility; otherwise, my answer will always be the same, and I will appear to be wasting the time of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree with you on that, General Radinovic. We are maybe wasting our time, but, however, please make an additional effort and try to answer direct questions to -- try to provide more direct answers to the questions by the Prosecutor. Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you said in your evidence in-chief, and you have done in your cross-examination, that you spoke to a number of individuals within the Bosnian Serb army before giving your testimony. Did you speak to General Mladic or Colonel Beara about what happened in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, no. Unfortunately, I was not able to reach them. I don't know where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We can move on to another area, now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you recall in your evidence that you stated that on the night of the 11th of July, a meeting took place at which General Mladic appointed General Krstic as the operational group commander, as the Commander of forces for the operation in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If an exhibit could be prepared, Exhibit 425.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, are you quite certain that that meeting took place on the 11th of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I'm not absolutely certain because I don't have the minutes from that meeting, nor do I have a document; but General Krstic spoke about that evening in his testimony -- about that meeting, I'm sorry, and I feel that his memory is probably reliable. And on the basis of the study I did of various documents for this testimony, I came to the conclusion that that could be the undisputed date when the meeting was held. But I repeat, I did not find a document on the basis of which I could be absolutely sure that that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, on the 13th of October of last year -- of this year, I'm sorry, an interview was conducted with Colonel Trivic who is the Commander of the Romanija Brigade, as you know. Do you know Colonel Trivic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Personally I don't know him, but I know that he was the Commander of the Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General, this is what he stated in his interview with the Office of the Prosecutor about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I assume that my learned friend Mr. Cayley will use a part of the interview that Colonel Trivic gave to the Prosecution; he told me he would do that prior to today's hearing. So it is an interview that Colonel Trivic had with the investigators of the Tribunal in Banja Luka on the 13th of October this year. We have already on two occasions witnessed the use of this interview by the Prosecution, mostly to check the credibility or impeach the witness. I objected, and the Trial Chamber made its ruling. I think that this time we have a completely different situation. This witness here will be submitted an exhibit which doesn't speak about something that the witness could have any personal knowledge about. Regarding the authenticity and verification of this exhibit, we were not able to state our position as we'd had no possibility to do so as it was not disclosed to us in advance, nor to check the truthfulness of any facts contained in this interview. If my learned colleague wishes to refer to an abstract situation that the witness refers to, he could do so in abstract terms, in theoretical terms, rather than referring to this exhibit, as the Defence has not had occasion to take a position on this exhibit, nor has the witness had access to it. So if a question is put to the witness regarding this exhibit, we object. If the Prosecution has a theoretical question to pose to the witness, we have nothing against; but not knowing the exact option of Mr. Cayley, I'm saying in advance that if this exhibit is used in concrete terms, the Defence will object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as the Bench knows already, Colonel Mirko Trivic was on the list of witnesses that the Defence intended to call. On that basis, I would assume that they had spoken to him if they were going to call him as a witness, and I would hope that if they have spoken to him, that what he told them is the same as what he told us. Secondly, this witness has stated that he spoke to a number of VRS officers. He had that opportunity in putting together his expert report. He spoke to a number of VRS officers who were engaged in this operation, and I would assume that he spoke to them about all of the facts which were relevant to his report, including the date of this meeting.
