All I wish to do is to put to the witness, to an expert witness, and I think it's perfectly fair since he's supposed to have considered all the evidence that is relevant to his report and this case, what Colonel Trivic's views were on that meeting that allegedly took place on the 11th of July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in order to do this, you're going to examine this document in detail or are you just going to use the information in general terms as suggested by Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Colonel Trivic makes a single assertion which I wish to put to the witness. It is a three-line assertion within his interview. Colonel Trivic was at the interview. That's what he told us. If that's to be believed, I think I can put that to the witness and see what his response was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic. To close the discussion, we have to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will be brief. We did talk to Colonel Trivic, but I'm not able to compare his statement with what the Prosecutor is now claiming just now. That is one point. Secondly, I think the Chamber also should have access to the whole interview so that they may ask questions of the General if the Prosecution is relying on the statement of Colonel Trivic. Thirdly, I still don't know how Colonel Trivic was interviewed, under which circumstances. Bearing all this in mind, we still maintain the objection that we have just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, the Chamber is of the opinion and decides that you should ask the witness whether he knows that Colonel Trivic said whatever it is you want to say. Regardless of the response, you're going to ask the question that you have to ask, but the Chamber wishes to inform you that the Chamber will not take as evidence what the statement itself says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand perfectly. In fact, Mr. Visnjic, I gave the wrong date for the interview. It was held on the 5th of October, 2000, not the 13th, as I stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, during that interview, it was put -- the following question was put to Colonel Trivic and it's as follows, "JR" standing for Mr. Ruez, the interviewer. JR. It is 1303 hours and we are resuming the interview with Colonel Trivic, so we are still on the meeting of the 12th of July after 10.00. During the interruption at one point, you told us that this meeting was also about giving -- giving, receiving new tasks, and the new task was to receive the new task towards Zepa. Would you please develop on that part of the meeting? GK: After the meeting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please read slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: GK: After the briefing, General Mladic issued an order to General Krstic to issue an order to regroup the forces to send them to Zepa. Now, General, it had previously been established during this interview - and it can be seen actually on page 47, Mr. Visnjic - that the meeting which you have stated took place on the 11th of July in fact took place on the 12th of July. Would you agree with me that Colonel Trivic would know better than you the date that this meeting took place when General Krstic was appointed to be the Commander of the forces in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He certainly knows better than me, but why should he know better than Krstic if Krstic said it was on the 11th in the evening. The meeting in the command of the Bratunac Brigade was held on the 11th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I don't think my learned friend wishes to make any objection, so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Did you want to say something, Mr. Visnjic? I saw you getting on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, as the witness has already given an answer. So we'll withdraw your objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. So continue, Mr. Cayley, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with Prosecutor's Exhibit 426.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you stated in your evidence that the operation towards Zepa was not referred to in directive 7/1. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I said that Stupcanica was not mentioned, that the Stupcanica 95 operation was not mentioned. Whether the enclaves were mentioned or not, whether I said they were or not, I really can't remember every word I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But directive 7/1 does refer, does it not, General, to combat operations towards the enclave of Zepa? It was anticipated by the Main Staff and by Mr. Karadzic in March of 1995 that there would be combat operations towards Zepa, wasn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: There's nothing illogical about that, bearing in mind the fact that these were enclaves from which the Muslim army was active, but my statement referred to the Stupcanica operation, as the coded name for the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when did General Krstic arrive at the forward command post in Krivace?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: In my testimony, I said that from the moment he was given the assignment to prepare, plan, and execute the operation Stupcanica 95, that is the Zepa operation, he could have been at various different places. From the forward command post in Pribicevac, that command post had to be dismantled, the installations removed, and then a new forward command post had to be set up at Krivace. I have no documents nor was I able from those available to me to ascertain with precision the direction of movement and his positions, where he was between Pribicevac and Krivace and back again, but I said that he might have been at Pribicevac, at Krivace, or at Vlasenica at the command post in order to carry out all the necessary activities required when planning, organising, and preparing an operation of this kind. And I also said that it was quite normal for him to also be in the area of the units which he planned to engage for Zepa to see what condition they were in, to establish personal contact with the Brigade Commanders, to tour the areas from which they would be deployed, to observe the axes upon which he would dispatch them. All of these are operations which a commander engages in when preparing and organising an operation. And indeed, I cannot tell you with precision when he appeared. I know when he should -- he must have appeared. That must have been at the time when he ordered combat readiness of communications at the command post. That was on the 13th by 1800 hours. This was what was written in his order, and he had to appear at that time to check whether the communications had been installed as they should have been, and that was for me a relevant fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, are you aware of what General Krstic stated that he did on the afternoon of the 13th of July before he arrived at the command post in Krivace?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, just as this moment I can't remember exactly what he said he did, but I know what he should have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He should have focussed on the operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- I'm not interested in what he should have done, I'm interested in what he did. And I can inform you that both General Krstic and a witness, Witness DA, stated that General Krstic spent the great proportion Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the 13th of July of 1995 visiting wounded soldiers and making social visits to members of his family. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, if General Krstic was making social visits on the day before an operation, you would agree with me that he was in fact taking advantage of a respite or a lull in activity before another major operation took place, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He issued assignments, and those preparatory activities were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, General, you're not answering my question, and I'll repeat it to you. If General Krstic, by his own words and by the words of his own witness, was making social visits on the 13th of July of 1995, the day before the Zepa operation was to commence, you would agree with me that he was in fact taking advantage of a respite or a lull in activity before another operation took place, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way. If you really insist on calling it that, yes. Touring the wounded is also an obligation of a senior officer. It is also officially prescribed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if you could have available before you paragraph 3.4 of your report, Defence Exhibit 160.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And it's on page 52 of both the English and the B/C/S version. If, Mr. Usher, you could move the document up. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General, you will find, I think, the relevant passage --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It is number, I beg your pardon, which page did you say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's page 52, General, line 16 of paragraph 3.4. And I will read what you stated: "To put it simply, it was impossible to assume the duty of Corps Commander, i.e., to assume responsibility for the situation in the entire Drina Corps zone of responsibility before necessary conditions for the transfer of duties were created. These conditions primarily mean a pause or respite in the fighting, and in this case it meant waiting for the end of Operation Zepa which was in full flow between July 15 and 20." Now, General, you have already acknowledged to me that the 13th of July was, in fact, a respite or a lull in the fighting. And I think based on your own reasoning, you would agree with me that the 13th of July of 1995 was an absolutely ideal time for command to pass from General Zivanovic to General Krstic, wasn't it, based on your own reasoning from that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, sir. That cannot be put like that because in the decree, the constituent act of the Supreme Commander, it is stated that the appointment is of the 15th of July --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: -- and no one has the right --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- we'll get to the discussion of that document and what you said about it. I will allow you to say all you wish to say about that document. What I want you to concentrate now is the reasoning in your report. That's all I want you to think about. You have agreed with me that the 13th of July of 1995 was a respite in the fighting. Now, based on your logic, General, based on your logic where you state that a pause or a respite in fighting was the ideal time for a change of command, would you not agree with me, General, that the 13th of July of 1995 was such a time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The 13th of July was not a pause in the operation, it was the eve of a new operation, and that time is not suitable for any kind of takeover of new duties. And he was appointed Commander of the Operative Group for Zepa. It was still in the preparatory stages. It had not even begun. But more importantly, it is a date that is not mentioned in the constituent document, and he was not authorised to take over duty on that date, nor was anyone authorised to hand over to him duty on that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 483. Now, General, this, and Your Honours, is the operations order for Stupcanica 95, the operation towards Zepa. Now, General, you have already testified on a number of occasions that General Krstic was appointed to command the Operative Group that was responsible for combat in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the front page -- the front page of that document is present on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, General Krstic wrote this order, and he states at the top of this order that it is an order from the Drina Corps Command, Krivace forward command post. Now, General, you would agree with me that any sensible military officer receiving a copy of this order would make the logical assumption that this was an order from the Corps Command and not from any kind of operative group command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: An operative group is a component part of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, isn't it the normal military convention for a commander to identify on an order that he is actually in command over -- you're not getting --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I apologise, I didn't hear you. There was an interruption in the interpretation, so could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it not normal military convention for a commander who is placed in command of an operative group, is placed in command of a subset of a larger unit, to actually identify that fact on the order that he issues?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but the problem is that there is no document from whoever designated General Krstic as Commander of the Operative Group, so no reference can be made to a document. And the rights that would emanate from that document of the person who is in command to call him the Commander of the Operative Group. You see that General Krstic signed this document as Chief of Staff, which means that he too acknowledged the fact that there is no document, no paper of his appointment, no written appointment for him to be able to use that title in communication. It was probably an oral order by the Commander of the Main Staff and there is no document that he can refer to and call himself the Commander of the Operative Group. So when I'm saying that General Krstic was the Commander of the Operative Group, what I'm saying is that he was in fact there conducting the operation following the oral order of the Commander of the Main Staff. That was his right. He could have issued a written document, but he need not have. But he appointed him Commander of the Operative Group. However, lacking the document, he cannot call himself the Commander of the Operative Group, but that is how he behaves although he doesn't sign any documents as the Commander of the Operative Group. It does have certain implications and limitations this fact. He did not behave completely autonomously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, so what you're saying to the Court is even though General Krstic knew when he wrote this order that in fact he was to be the Commander of an Operative Group going to Zepa, he represented to the entire Drina Corps that the Drina Corps Command was to move to Krivace and that this was to be a Drina Corps operation. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: What I am saying is that from the end of the Srebrenica operation a new forward command post is being formed of the Drina Corps from which the operative group conducting the operation for Zepa is being commanded. That is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let's go to paragraph 10 of this order. That is on page 4 of the English translation and it is on page 4 of your version. Now, General, it states here, this order signed by General Krstic, that the Drina Corps forward command post in Krivace shall start work at 1800 hours on the 13th of July of 1995. Now, General, you would agree with me that General Krstic makes no reference in this order to an operative group forward command post moving to Zepa, does he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He mentions the forward command post of the Drina Corps, but he does not mention the operative group because he doesn't have a document on the basis of which he can call himself Commander of the Operative Group. He's the authorised officer of the Drina Corps at the forward command post commanding the forces on Zepa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you yourself, throughout your evidence, have stated - and, Mr. Visnjic, this is at page 7905 a single example of it - that it is a very strict requirement that the commander of the corps be at the forward command post. You have stated that in your evidence, haven't you, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. No. No, it's not a very strict regulation. The Corps Commander may, on the basis of his own judgement, appear at the forward command post. It is up to him, to his own judgement, where he should be at what point in time, where his appearance is most important. If he considers it to be at the forward command post, that is where he will go. If not, then he will not go there. There are twofold implications of this being the fact that the Commander of the Main Staff of the VRS ordered General Krstic to carry out the operation on Zepa, thereby in practice and in fact, he relieved the Corps Commander of the obligation to appear at the forward command post, whereas Krstic was obliged to be there as the commander of the group conducting the operation. So that is the distinction between this situation and the situation at the forward command post in Pribicevac. There the commander was obliged to appear even though General Krstic, as Chief of Staff, was at the forward command post. In this case it is different. General Krstic has the duty to conduct the operation and General Zivanovic has no obligation to appear at the forward command post. It would have been no error on his part if he had appeared because he continues to be Corps Commander. So it would not have been a mistake nor any infringement of Krstic's rights as commander of the forces engaged for the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 762, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, here you see an order from a Colonel Vladimir Arsic, and you will see at the top that Colonel Arsic particularly refers to being in command of an operative group, of Doboj Operative Group, and he is himself giving commands to a tactical group. Now, bearing in mind, General, that it was in fact a requirement to identify that a commander was in command of an operative group as opposed to an entire corps, don't you think that General Krstic, being an experienced VRS officer, would have actually put that fact in this order had he really believed that he was in command of an operative group rather than the entire corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily, for the simple reason that General Krstic was Chief of Staff and also Deputy Commander. Even if General Mladic had not given him orders to carry out that operation, the Corps Commander could have given him that order. He could have said, "Krstic, from now on you will plan and carry out the Zepa operation as an operation carried out by such-and-such a group," and he could designate the forces. As you can see from the combat order for Zepa, General Krstic issued that document to all units of the Drina Corps which he wished to engage for Zepa without any limitations because in the order for Zepa, nobody had given him the exact units he had to engage. He had the freedom to select them himself. If the Commander of the Main Staff had wanted him to form an operative group first as a provisional formation and to use it for Zepa, he would have done so, but he didn't think it necessary, but, rather, he authorised him to include in that group whoever he thought he should include and to act accordingly. So the order for Zepa, in the sense of command, is specific insofar that General Krstic was told to control and command the forces for Zepa, that is, first to prepare and organise the Zepa operation and to carrying out -- to carry it out from its beginning until the end. And this is very important to note because this throws very fixed -- clear right on his command responsibility from the 11th in the evening until the 20th when he actually took over the duty of Corps Commander. That is why this is important. But there can be no analogy with this document because Krstic was Deputy Commander of the whole Drina Corps, of the whole Drina Corps. He could have even been assigned -- he could even have assigned a tactical group to carry out a certain task without prior orders how to form that tactical group. So that was the right of command that General Krstic had as Deputy Commander, that he may engage in different types of assignments within the area of the zone of responsibility of the corps. The Commander of the Main Staff decided to appoint him to be commander. The Corps Commander agreed or not or whatever, that's another matter, and General Krstic prepared and carried out the Zepa operation, and it is in that context that his responsibility and -- command responsibility should be viewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, at page 7905 of your evidence, you said: "There is a very strict requirement that the commander should be located at the forward command post because that is the very reason why the command is being relocated because it is so that the commander can have a more efficient control over his troops from the forward command post." Now, General, based on your logic and based on the fact that the Zepa operations order identifies Krivace as the forward command post, based on the fact that General Zivanovic was never seen at the forward command post in Krivace, based on the evidence that the Judges have heard, you would agree with me that it is a logical conclusion that General Krstic was the Commander of the Drina Corps from the 13th of July of 1995, wouldn't you, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. I would not agree with you because standing in the way is the decree of the president of the republic and my overall insight into the course of events from the 12th until the 20th. There is not a single document on the basis of which it is possible to conclude that General Zivanovic was replaced, that he was removed from duty, or that he was sick or wounded, that he was unable to perform his duties. I really did not come across any such document, and therefore I have no reason to believe that General Krstic became commander before he took over duty from Zivanovic and before that is done in the regular way in which duty is transferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley, perhaps it is now time for a break. We'll now have a 50-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 759, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I just want some information from General Radinovic. General, you were mentioning that till the 20th, General Krstic did not take over any duty from Zivanovic. Concerning Zivanovic, was there any real role played by him during this period, basic roles between the 11th and the 20th, or was he a little bit absent from the picture according to your assessment? Just a general question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any information as to whether he was removed from duty at that time, so I couldn't comment on that aspect of your question; however, there are documents which he signed on the 13th of July which indicates that he was still active within the chain of command. There are certain activities which are being conducted within the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps which are not directly part of the Zepa operation, although they do affect the operative situation in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade; that is, that situation affects the issue of the Zepa operation because General Krstic expected certain forces to be returned to him. So that, to a certain extent, affects the situation in Zepa. However, in the Drina Corps area of responsibility, as of the 13th of July, there is a number of operative problems which General Zivanovic had to busy himself with, and my assumption was that he was indeed involved in dealing with those problems because there are no documents which would indicate that he was not active. First of all, I think of the necessity to prevent the breakthrough of the 28th Division from the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, in particular, area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, and also on the points of contact between the Zvornik Brigade and the Birac Brigade. And he was also involved with the prevention of the breakthrough of the BiH army forces, that is its 2nd Corps, from the direction of Tuzla in an attempt to link up with the forces attempting the breakthrough from Srebrenica. So that is quite a number of duties for the Commander of the Drina Corps to still behave as an active participant in the chain of command. And since I do not have any documents which would exclude him from the picture, I have to assume that he was still part of that chain of command at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, General. But you say you have no documents to prove -- which prove that he was excluded from the picture, but do you have documents which prove that he was included in the picture? Not passively, actively.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: By definition, he is participating in the command. He's both de facto and nominally the Commander of the Drina Corps until such a time as he hands over the duty of command and until a document is issued to that effect. So he is here de jure and de facto Commander of the Corps, and by definition he has this command duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: By definition, that's right, but there is nothing concrete, no orders signed by him and so on. That's just my question. Did you come across orders signed by him in this period, by Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. General Zivanovic signed an order on the 13th as the corps commander, and he is, of course, in the area of responsibility of the corps and he's active. He also signed an order on the 14th, I believe, or maybe even on a later date - I don't remember exactly when - whereby he is requesting his subordinate officers as to when the hand-over of duty can take place in the usual manner, which means that he was still in the area of responsibility. And as long as he was able to command the corps both physically and formally, he was still on duty as a commander. As to how active he was, it's a matter of his assessment. I don't know whether it was necessary to issue specific documents of command. All of the units which were carrying out their missions in the area, particularly Zvornik and Birac Brigade, they were at their positions and they were engaged in combat with the forces of the 28th Division which were attempting a breakthrough from the area. So there was no need for him to make any radical changes with new orders. He was dealing with the current situation, with the situation that was on the ground at that time by inspecting the units that were deployed in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if you could look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 759 in front of you, and if you could look at the -- it's two orders. If you could look at the order on the left-hand side, the order that's signed by General Zivanovic, which can be seen on the ELMO at the moment. General, based on this order of the 12th of July of 1995, who was the Commander of the Drina Corps on that date?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: The Commander of the Drina Corps was General Zivanovic, who was the commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, if the booth can bring in the focus of that document so we could see both documents alongside each other. If you could move it a little bit. If the booth could focus in. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, now looking at the document on the right-hand side which is dated the 13th of July, 1995, which you will note is identical in all respects, it says at the top, "Command of the Drina Corps," as per the order of General Zivanovic, and it is signed at the bottom "Commander, Major-General Radislav Krstic." Now, on the basis of the order of the 13th of July, 1995, you would agree with me that General Krstic is here representing himself as the Commander of the Drina Corps, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Only for the purposes of this document. This document concerns the search of terrain for the Milici and Bratunac Brigades and the Skelani Battalion. Those are the units which General Krstic included in his group for Zepa, and the order in question concerns the search of terrain. As to why we see the word "Commander" here there can be several interpretations, but it obviously refers to his command function within the preparation for the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me that at the top of both documents, the Zivanovic document and the Krstic document, it states "Command of the Drina Corps"? Does it say exactly the same thing at the top of both documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, it's the same formation. Both Krstic and Zivanovic belonged to the Drina Corps, and they issued their orders on behalf of the Drina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we go to the signature block on both documents, and, Mr. Usher, if you could move the document to the right slightly. Across a bit further. Perfect. If the focus could come out a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if we look at the signature block of each document, you'd agree with me that General Zivanovic signs as commander and indeed General Krstic signs as commander, does he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Well, Krstic is also the commander at that time. He's the Commander of the Zepa Operative Group and he's issuing an order to the units which are part of that operative group. So he's a commander as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, does this order of the 13th of July of General Krstic make any reference to the Operative Group of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, but you have to bear in mind the done text in which all this is taking place. The document was issued in the context of the preparations for the Zepa operation by General Krstic. If we want to be mindful of the facts, and I hope we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can you examine the top of this document where it states "Command of the Drina Corps"? Now I'm referring to General Krstic's order. Underneath "Command of the Drina Corps" it says, "Strictly Confidential, number 01/4-157-5." It's a fact, isn't it, General, that the designation "01" refers to the Commander of the Corps, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: It's a convention. It need not necessarily be so. Well, Krstic was the commander, the Commander of the Operative Group, and he has the right to use this mark. And even if he had used number "2", it wouldn't have been a mistake. But since he was appointed by the Commander of the Main Staff to command the forces engaged in Zepa, he has the right to use number "1".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your evidence, General, is that even though General Krstic represents himself in this order as the Commander of the Drina Corps, even though convention demands that "01" apply only to the Commander of the Drina Corps, that everybody knew on reading this order that in fact he wasn't the Commander of the Drina Corps at all. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: "01" refers to the commander as such, not the Commander of the Drina Corps. Every commander marks, designates his documents with 01, the Commander of the Main Staff, the Brigade Commander, Corps Commander. This is a convention concerning this type of designation so that the documents can be easily traced. General Krstic used his right here in this document. He was indeed appointed as the commander and he functioned as the commander of that part of the corps which was involved in the preparations for the Zepa operation, and it was in that capacity that he issued this document. If I had written this document, I wouldn't have used this particular designation. So from this you can see that to a certain extent, he overstepped his duties, and he made a certain change by acting this way in the system of command because it is obvious that he was not the Corps Commander because there is a document which was signed by Zivanovic in his capacity of Corps Commander on the same date. So if we bear in mind the relevant decree whereby he was appointed commander, it is obvious that he did not act here in his capacity as the Corps Commander. There are several facts pointing to the conclusion that this order was not issued in his capacity as the Drina Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you suggesting to the Court that General Krstic essentially misrepresented himself in this order; by using this designation of the commander, 01, he was in fact misrepresenting himself to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. What I stated, sir, was that within the same command, to use one and the same designation for two individuals and for two positions is not a very good idea for the overall system of command, that this is not something I would have done. However, he did not commit any serious infringement of the system of command. He was indeed the Commander of the Zepa forces, and he was able to use this designation, but I wouldn't have used it myself, for example. He signed the Zepa order as the chief of staff. I could have signed this document as a chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, are you aware that the last order signed by General Zivanovic was at 1720 on the 13th of July of 1995, and the first order signed by General Krstic was at 2000 hours as commander on the 13th of July, 1995? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but do you really believe that a change in the function of the Corps Commander could occur in such a short period of time? All the more so because we have a document stating when the change is only allowed to take place by the 15th of July, pursuant to the document. The hand-over, the takeover duty cannot take place. The Supreme Commander was explicit in saying that the appointment was to take place, was to come into effect with the date of the 15th of July. Any document that General Krstic would have issued as Corps Commander prior to that date would be null and void, and he would have to suffer all consequences for that, political and military consequences. And legally speaking, such a document would have been null and void because he was not the Corps Commander at the time, and he did not have authority from the only instance which is empowered to appoint him as Corps Commander, to act in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General, but if the order has been implemented without any protest, wouldn't that be an admission that he is the Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He is both Chief of Staff and Deputy Corps Commander. So as regards the continuity of command, it is not necessary for him to attribute to himself those functions for which he was not authorised. He has the right to replace the commander and to assume the command when the commander is unavailable. It was not necessary for him to attribute to himself the function of the Corps Commander when that was -- when it was not necessary for him to do that. So he could only sign this document as the Commander for the Zepa forces. However, since we have the mention of the brigades, the Bratunac, Milici Brigades and the Skelani Battalion who were involved in the search of the terrain, this actually concerns only the portion of the forces over which he was given the command, namely, the forces that were to be committed for the purposes of the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if you could please turn to page 51 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's Defence Exhibit 160.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Fifty, what did you say, I'm sorry, what page?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 51, General. Now, General, my understanding from your report, you give two principle reasons why General Krstic signed Prosecutor's Exhibit 463 in the manner in which he did, that of commander, and I will read to you the first reason that you give. "The fact that there are some documents signed by Krstic before July 15th can be interpreted in two ways. First, that Krstic issued and signed these documents in the role of deputy commander, having simply overlooked the fact that the place for the signature is marked 'Commander,' instead of 'Deputy Commander'." Now, General, you agree with me, you would agree with me, that had General Krstic intended to represent himself as the deputy commander, he would have said so, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but you omitted to read what follows and which provides the explanation for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we'll move on to the explanation in a moment. If you just answer my question: If General Krstic had intended to represent himself as the deputy commander, he would have put that in the order, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He would have if he had looked. Maybe he didn't look closely. And he considered himself a commander, and it wouldn't make any difference because in terms of competencies, nothing substantial changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But General, General Krstic was a professional, intelligent officer. He would not have signed a document, would he, as commander, if he had meant to sign it as deputy commander, would he?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 760 ready.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As you see, he did, even though he was not the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here, General, is an order of the 11th of December, 1994, in which General Krstic signs off as the Deputy Commander. Do you see that at the bottom of the order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you'd agree with me based on this order, Prosecutor's Exhibit 760 where General Krstic signs as deputy commander and on the basis of the order that we're discussing at the moment, 463, where General Krstic signs as the commander, he knew the distinction between those two roles and he indeed ensured in his orders that he properly represented himself, didn't he, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He knew that he was Commander of the forces for Zepa and that is why he signed in that way. But I agree with you that he knew the difference. So in answer to your question, the answer is yes. But he knew that he was Commander of the Operative Group for Zepa and it is in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that capacity that he signed that other document. But in answer to your question just now, my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, the second reason that you gave in your report, and I will read the section that you wanted me to read, "Second" -- it is the second plausible reason that you give for Krstic signing that document as commander: "Second that Krstic signed documents as "commander" and not as "deputy commander" or "chief of staff" without authorisation." Now, General, you would agree with me that had General Krstic been signing an order as commander on behalf of General Zivanovic, he would have said so, wouldn't he, in the order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes, but he signed this order in his own name as commander of the group for Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if Prosecutor's Exhibit 76 could be placed on the ELMO. I'm sorry, Defence Exhibit 76. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 76/A bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, here is an order which you will agree was signed by General Krstic on behalf of General Zivanovic. And before you question the document, that is the signature of General Krstic. Here we see General Krstic expressly stating in an order that he was signing on behalf of General Zivanovic. So you'd agree with me, General, that from this document, General Krstic knew when he was signing on behalf of the Corps Commander because he would say so in the order, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Yes. He knew that he was signing in the -- when he was signing in the role of commander and when in the role of deputy commander, and that is why for Zepa, for the search operation, he signed it in the role of commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, if we accept that General Krstic knew when he was signing as deputy commander, if he knew when he was signing on behalf of somebody else, and there is absolutely no reference to the operational group for Zepa obtained in Prosecutor's Exhibit Exhibit 463, you'd agree with me that on the basis of those three facts General Krstic was signing as the Commander of the Drina Corps, wasn't he, on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I have told you several times that I do not agree with your conclusion and my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you stated earlier that had General Krstic indeed misrepresented himself as the Commander of the Drina Corps then that order would have been null and void. Do you recall that evidence? In fact, I think His Honour Judge Riad asked you about that particular point.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. No, no. I said that the order would have consequences. Every time Krstic, in any capacity, signs an act, a document, that document produces consequences because he is by function Chief of Staff and deputy commander. So every document he signs produces consequences, but only within the framework and within the context of the document he has issued. But in legal terms, if he signs as a commander and an expert establishes that he was not the commander, then in legal terms it would be null and void. That is the distinction I wanted to make. What I want to say is that General Krstic had no need to attach to his name titles that don't belong to him because being the deputy commander he has the right to issue orders whenever the commander is absent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you state that General Krstic signed this order in the capacity as Commander of the Zepa operation, and you also referred to the fact that the order, Prosecutor's Exhibit 463, gave orders to the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, and the Skelani Battalion. Are you aware, General, that the Skelani Battalion was never engaged in the operation towards Zepa? It was not part of those forces that were engaged towards Zepa. On that basis, General, if General Krstic was giving orders to those units that did not comprise the Operative Group Zepa, he was giving orders to the rest of the corps and on that basis, General, he was the commander of the corps, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He issued an order here to the Milici Brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, and the Skelani Battalion. Only a part of those forces was included in the operative group for Zepa. Not all those forces. But within the preparations and the regrouping of forces for the Zepa operation, it was necessary to search the terrain in order to secure the rear. And in this part of the assignment, the preparatory work for the Zepa operation, the Skelani Battalion did participate on the left side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if General Krstic only had authority for those forces engaged in the Zepa operation, how did he have authority to issue orders to the Skelani Battalion? How did he have authority until he was the Commander of the Drina Corps, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: There seems to be a basic misunderstanding between us. By General Krstic's appointment by General Mladic as commander of the group which was to carry out the Zepa operation, General Krstic did not explicitly by any specific document -- he was not removed from the duty of Chief of Staff and Deputy Commander of the Drina Corps. In military terms, he was decommanded; that is, he was given the duty to carry out the next operation. No one deprived him of the authority he had as Deputy of the Drina Corps. The only thing is that he didn't have to participate in those activities which were outside the area of responsibility of Zepa. So he was not disempowered. In spite of the fact that General Krstic was engaged in Zepa, you have no newly appointed Chief of Staff. Colonel Andric will become Chief of Staff once the Zepa operation was completed. So that position was not eliminated but it wasn't in active operation while General Krstic was Commander of the Zepa operation. You have to have that in mind. So there was no one who prohibited General Krstic from using the Skelani battalion to search the terrain and to carry out preparations for the subsequent operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you just stated in your evidence, General, that the only thing that General Krstic didn't have to participate in were those activities which were outside the area of responsibility of Zepa, but you would agree with me if he was issuing orders to the Skelani Battalion, the Bratunac Brigade, and the Milici Brigade, who were all involved in operations in Srebrenica, he was giving orders, wasn't he, to activities outside Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: This area we are referring to is an area that was directly included in the operations area of Zepa. When an operation is being prepared, then the area or zone of deployment of units is not marked by lines. It is an area that has its depth, and the depth of the brigade on the offensive is 10 to 15 kilometres. So it's not just the front line and the units on the front line but the whole combat formation for attack which entails the rear, the depth; and that area certainly includes the area where the Skelani Battalion was searching the terrain, as well as the Milici and Bratunac Brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is Ravni Buljin in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That is the border of the Srebrenica enclave. If you're talking about Buljim, Ravni Buljim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Zeleni Jadar just south of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That also is the border. It is along the border. That is the border area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you know whether or not this order was actually complied with, Prosecutor's Exhibit 463?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: You mean search of the terrain? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Units of the Bratunac and Milici Brigades and the Skelani Battalion certainly did carry out their assignment regarding searching the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Prosecutor's Exhibit 464 could be placed in front of the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I have a question for you. Generally speaking, if General Krstic was to replace Zivanovic as Corps Commander, how would he sign an order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He could sign the order in several -- he had several options. He could put his signature under a title called "Corps Commander," and all his subordinates know his subject and on that basis can easily know whether the order was signed by an authorised official or not. Another possibility, another option, would be for him to put "representing the commander," or to say "deputy commander," or to say "chief of staff of the command." In all those capacities, operationally and in factual and legal terms, the effect of the document would be identical: He would always be the authorised official of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of these four possibilities, which would be more in line with the rules? Are they all equal, or is there one that is preferred?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: If we exclude this particular document, if we're talking in principle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'm now excluding this particular document, but we're talking in general terms. In a normal situation, he's Chief of Staff and Deputy Commander, and he needs to sign an order of the command in the absence of General Zivanovic. It is this situation that I should like you to address. You have mentioned four options, and my question is, is there one out of the four that is more in conformity with the rules, or are they all equal?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As far as the consequences are concerned and the authority, they are identical, but the normal thing would be for him to refer to the function that he has in the structure of the command of the Drina Corps, and that is Chief of Staff. Everyone knows automatically that he is also Deputy Commander, so it would be sufficient for him to say Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Cayley, you may continue. Judge Fouad Riad has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just a question on the practical level. How did he always sign, with the exception of this order where he signed "commander"? Did he ever sign -- as you said, he could sign "commander" and everybody knew his signature. Did he do it, or was it also "deputy commander" with the exception of this one? According to your analysis and what you saw.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: According to what I saw, he signed in all three variants. There are documents signed as chief of staff; there are documents he signed as deputy commander; and there are also documents he signed under the heading "commander," and he added the word "for" the little word "for," which means he's acting on behalf of somebody, that he has the authority to do that. So he signed in all three ways. The most natural, the most normal way for him to sign would be as Chief of Staff because everyone knows that that is what he was, everyone knows his signature, and there's absolutely no obstacle to carry out those command documents that he signed as Chief of Staff because it is known that he has the authority to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So at best, if he's commander, he would sign "for," he would put "for" before it, "for" the commander? And he never signed "commander" except in this document without putting "for"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In official correspondence in the JNA or the army of Republika Srpska when before the heading "commander" you put the word "for," it signified that somebody is signing the document who is representing the commander at that particular point in time. So one might say that he is signing on behalf of the commander when he says "for" and not as the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's what I mean, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with Prosecutor's Exhibit 465. It is a map. If you don't have it to hand, Madam Registrar, I can .... If you could move that map up a little bit please, Mr. Usher. A bit further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, Prosecutor's Exhibit 463, General Krstic's order to the Bratunac Brigade, Milici Brigade, and the Skelani Independent Battalion, identifies certain locations from which the search was to be carried out. Could you please point on that map, General, to Ravni Buljim? And this is the orders in respect of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Ravni Buljim is in the northwestern corner of the enclave. The next location is down towards Zvijezda which I think you'll find in the centre, General, of the enclave. If you could point to that, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Zvijezda?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So Zvijezda is in the middle of the enclave? Siljato Brdo, could you point to that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Siljato Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slapovici and Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, those were the lines up to which the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade were to search, and would you agree with me, General, that they stretch essentially from the top to the bottom of the enclave, don't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: But Krstic was not broadening the area, it was the brigade commander who was. Krstic, in his order, ordered which part of the area should be searched, and in military terms, the cleaning of the terrain. I don't see what the dispute is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as we're talking about these geographic names, perhaps it would be simpler to give the witness the document, the document Mr. Cayley is referring to. I'm referring to Exhibit 463. I think that's what we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, I don't quite get the question. Do you have a response?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought the witness already had that document. If Mr. Visnjic is indicating that he doesn't, then we should give it to him. It doesn't need to be placed on the ELMO. It's better that the witness has the document. He has it already. I thought he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, in essence you'd agree with me that General Krstic was giving an order for the search of the area enclosed by the Srebrenica enclave, wasn't he, in this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: But, sir, the area for the search of the terrain does not, strictly speaking, coincide with the borders of the enclave. The area of the enclave is approximately defined so that the brigades should know what is being referred to. The area of the Srebrenica enclave was mentioned so as to specify which particular areas do not -- are not included in the search area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is General Krstic issuing an order for the search of the enclave? Yes or no. It's very simple. You can see the locations on the map. Was he issuing an order for the search of the enclave or was he not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: When an order is being issued, then the most precise designations are lines and axes. A brigade cannot be limited to an area which it cannot fit into. You indicate the axes of the search. That is how a document like this is drafted. And I agree with you that in this order signed by Krstic it is stated that it is the enclave, that the duty to search the terrain does relate to the enclave area, to the area of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have Prosecutor's Exhibit 534 at hand, please? Now, General, the order issued by General Krstic, the order that we're having this lengthy discussion about, the number of that order was 01/4-157-5.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the order which General Krstic signs as commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this General, is a document from the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, dated the 14th of July, and I will just read three lines of paragraph 2: "Our forces are searching and clearing the terrain in accordance with order, strictly confidential number 01/4-157/5, and part of our forces is participating from our side in the encirclement of enemy forces at point 1." Now, General, you would agree with me that Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic, the Commander of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, was reporting back to the Drina Corps on the 14th of July, that he was complying with Krstic's, order, then he certainly believed that General Krstic was the Commander of the Drina Corps on the 14th of July, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with you because I still abide by the arguments that I have presented and that is that General Krstic, on the 14th, was not the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, General, you would agree with me that if Colonel Blagojevic believed that General Krstic was misrepresenting himself as the Commander of the Drina Corps, he would not have followed the order, would he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: If General Krstic was misrepresenting himself, he knows very well who General Krstic is, and there is no need for Krstic to introduce himself to him. He knows him. And he got an order from General Krstic, and he's carrying out that order. The only thing is that he expanded the area of responsibility beyond what he was ordered to do by General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the General could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 467, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the rank of General Krstic at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: At that time when he received this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, on the 13th of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: His primary function was commander of the forces on Zepa because the Zepa operation had already started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the rank, the military rank.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He was Major-General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the 11th of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: On the 11th of December, 1994. Let me try and recollect. I think he was Colonel. I think he was Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have Prosecutor's Exhibit 467 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And if the translation could be placed on the ELMO. Your Honours, this is a document that you may recall was written by hand by Colonel Blagojevic, and he put the date of the 14th of July on this document in his own hand. When the document was processed and sent by the army telegrapher, the date 17th of July was placed on that document, although, in fact, the document is signed as sent on the 14th of July at the end. So that is why there is a discrepancy in the dates on the document you see on the screen and the document the General has, which is dated the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this is a document that you can see is have Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic to the Command of the Drina Corps, and I will read it out: "We wish to inform you that we shall be able to secure the presence of the command and representatives of the municipal authorities for the official farewell for General Zivanovic, hitherto Commander of the Drina Corps, at 1300 hours on 23 June 1995." Now, General, you'd agree with me that based on this document Colonel Blagojevic believed, on the 14th of July of 1995, that General Zivanovic was no longer the Commander of the Drina Corps, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me that when a colonel in the Bosnian Serb army refers to General Zivanovic as the "hitherto," "the hitherto Commander of the Drina Corps," that he believes in his mind that General Zivanovic is no longer the Commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: That is not the -- up to the Brigade Commander to judge of his own free will who is the Corps Commander and who is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm not asking you that question. The question is a very simple one. Based on this document, based on this document, does Colonel Blagojevic represent his view as being that General Zivanovic is no longer the Commander of the Drina Corps? If you wish to decline to answer, then simply say, "I do not wish to answer," and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I have given you my answer that I disagree with you, because in the next sentence of this same document it says that Colonel Blagojevic has informed that members of his command will be able to attend the official farewell, and it is an official farewell where the former commander hands over duty and the new commander takes over. Until that moment, the former commander is still on duty. And you have also the decree of the president of the republic which says that until the 15th, no one has the right to transfer duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your position is, General, that essentially General Krstic was basically misrepresenting himself as the Corps Commander on the 13th of July and Colonel Blagojevic, one of his immediate subordinate commanders, was completely confused as to the situation and was referring erroneously to Zivanovic being the hitherto Commander of the Drina Corps. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He is the hitherto commander. Until then he was the commander. He was always the commander, and he didn't leave. He will leave only once that official farewell has taken place. That is how it is called according to the terminology of the transfer of duty. Corps Commanders and members of the senior commands transfer duty at an official meeting, at a working meeting which has an official and ceremonious character. And commanders of tactical units do the takeover and hand-over duty in front of lined-up units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Cayley. Just a question since you mentioned it. In English it is "hitherto," and in the French it's "jusqu'a present." I listened to it. It's "jusqu'a present." It means that he was still in command. "Jusqu'a present," it does not mean it is the final point. Is it in English or in French?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In the English language, it's a very old fashioned word, "hitherto," but it essentially means the previous commander, the person who was in the position and no longer is in the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because it is translated in French "jusqu'a present." When I say I am a Judge jusqu'a present, it means that I am still a Judge. So there must be -- we have first corrected the word. I know it is old English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The English translation of this document from the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Let's check it first.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We will, but there has been, to be honest with you, Judge Riad, there has been a lot of discussion about this particular word, so it's not something that we've just sort of pulled out of a hat. It's been interpreted as the word "hitherto," and I've just explained, I think it's clear what that word means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the French is not correct, in my opinion. "Jusqu'a present," the present is included. So if we rely -- just I wanted to understand. Otherwise, the President is listening in French, I'm listening in English; we will not have the same opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, are you going to suggest a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think perhaps it would be most opportune to ask the interpreters for an official commentary because we also have a dilemma, together with our learned friends from the Prosecution, which would be the best word in English, and I am not sure that this is the best solution for the Prosecution or the Defence. So perhaps the translation service could give us an additional explanation as to the various meanings that can be given to this word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. I think Mr. Cayley suggested that, too, when Mr. Cayley said that there was a discussion and that we will have the result of that linguistic discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, as far as the English-B/C/S version is concerned, and I believe my learned friend is already aware of this, there has been a report produced on that - in fact, copied to my learned friend Mr. Harmon - and I can read that into the record if you wish, or I can give you this to read. It simply says, "On the 31 October 2000 in the trial session of the case of The Prosecutor v. Krstic, General Krstic read OTP Exhibit 467/b in Serbian for the record. "The English booth interpreted the words of General Krstic as follows: `We wish to inform you that we are able to ensure the presence of members of the command and representatives of the municipal authorities for the official farewell for General Zivanovic, the outgoing commander of the Drina Corps, on 23rd of June 1995 at 1300 hours." And then this is the commentary by Maya Drazenovic-Carrieri, the chief of the interpretation service, she says the following: "At the request of the Prosecutor, I have reviewed the English transcript of the proceedings together with Exhibit 467/a. I wish to state for the record that the official translation of the Serbian term," which I shall probably mispronounce, "'dosadasnji' is `hitherto' as can be seen in the revised English translation (OTP Exhibit 467/a)." So we do for the purposes of the proceedings have the authoritative version of the English-Serbian version, but not on the French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have any comment from the translation service for the French as well, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll seek that commentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us now have a very brief break so that we can work until three. We'll have a 10-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I now want to move on to general principles of appointment of senior officers. Now, I want to read to you some evidence of a Defence witness, Witness DB, who is a serving senior VRS officer who testified before the Court, and my learned friend Mr. Harmon was asking him a number of questions about presidential decrees and appointments of officers, and the question went like this, General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that there was a presidential decree and the presidential decree was required for a number of positions, officer positions, but can you allow for the possibility that de facto someone assumes command prior to the issuance of a piece of paper signed by the president which formally designates the individual to a command post? And the answer to that question was, "I accept that possibility." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is on page 7281 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me, General, wouldn't you, that if a senior VRS officer stated in this courtroom that individuals could be appointed to de facto positions without the issuance of official paperwork, then that is a real possibility, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I think I'm more familiar with the matters than the officer who testified here, and I know that that cannot happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 468.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you yourself said in evidence, and this is at -- actually, I don't have the page reference for this at the moment, but I will give it to you when I can locate it. These are your words, "It is perfectly customary for those individuals," and here you were referring to senior officers, "to be discussed and assessed during high level meetings, and it is quite possible that the appointment in question was a kind of assessment of the personnel situation, human resources situation, and then the service in charge of drafting such documents then prepare the relevant documents on the 14th of July, 1995." Now, General, you yourself have stated in evidence that appointments could be made prior to the paperwork being issued. That is what you were saying then, wasn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sure I didn't state that. It is the process of assessing the personnel matters which takes place before the actual appointment. Human resources need to be managed and certain plans have to be made in respect of that. So before the actual appointment takes place the nominees, the candidates, are being assessed and they are being discussed at various meetings. Once an agreement is reached to that effect, then appropriate tasks are issued to the service, personnel services, which are in charge of drafting the actual document. But they are given specific instructions as to the relevant dates. They have no authority to determine dates, appointment dates, as they please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the Bosnian Serb army during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the Bosnian Serb documentary processes, how they processed appointments? Did you have anything to do with that at all, General, during the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: Me personally you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would agree with me on that basis that Witness DB, who was a senior officer in the VRS serving in Bosnia throughout the war, would have a much better idea than you as to whether or not de facto appointments were made without the paperwork being completed immediately?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: As regards the appointment of generals, I'm a hundred per cent sure he doesn't have any better knowledge than me of the issue, despite the fact that he was a member of the VRS and I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 536.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, as you can see, this is a daily combat report of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, and in paragraph 2 of this order, it states: "Our forces are still searching the terrain in accordance with your strictly confidential order number 01/4-157/5, dated 13 July 1995," and then he states the area of the search. Now, you would agree with me, General, that on the 15th of July, Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic is still executing General Krstic's order of the 13th of July of 1995 which General Krstic signs as the Commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He was carrying out the order which General Krstic signed as the Commander of the Zepa forces on the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you see that the order is addressed to the Command of the Drina Corps, forward command post of the Drina Corps? Do you see that on this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I see it on the document, but it only supports my position and not yours, that it was sent to the Drina Corps Command and the forward command post of the Drina Corps. There was no -- if there had been no need to send it to the forward command post, then no such mention would be made on the document. So this is sent to the person -- to the organ who is supposed to carry out the order, and it is sent to the Commander of the Drina Corps who is at the forward command post of the Drina Corps as the Commander of the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, where did Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic believe the forward command post of the Drina Corps was located, based on this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: He knows exactly where the forward command post is because in his order of the 13th of July regarding Zepa, General Krstic notified him of the location of the forward command post which was at Krivace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you have stated in your evidence that General Blagojevic sent this document to the Commander of the Drina Corps who is at the forward command post of the Drina Corps. You then go on and contradict yourself and say as the Commander of the Zepa operation. Now, upon the basis that General Zivanovic was never seen at the forward command post in Krivace, who was General -- who was Colonel Blagojevic referring this order to at Krivace, at the forward command post of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Continued]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir, whether my words are being misinterpreted by the interpretation service or by yourself. What I said was that the Commander of the Bratunac Brigade sent this report to the Command of the Drina Corps, to the location of the command, that is, at Vlasenica, and also to the forward command post of the Drina Corps at Krivace, namely, to General Krstic who had ordered him to do so explicitly. So he sent it both to the Drina Corps Command at Vlasenica and the Command of the Zepa Operative Group at the forward command post of the corps. That is how it is being done in this system of command, which may be complicated but that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
